# The MapSmith Manifesto

Ask an AI agent for a map and you will probably get one. Ask it whether the
numbers on that map are correct, and the honest answer is usually: nobody
knows. The geometry came out of a language model, the CRS was assumed, the
join was described rather than executed. It looks professional. That is the
problem.

MapSmith exists because *looks right* is not a standard anyone can sign their
name under. These are the commitments that follow from taking that seriously.

## 1. Engines compute. Models orchestrate.

Every geometry and every number in a MapSmith result comes from executing a
deterministic engine — GDAL, GeoPandas, DuckDB Spatial, Whitebox Workflows,
SedonaDB. None
of it is generated by a model, ever. The model's job is to decide *what* to
run; it is never asked to produce a coordinate. This is the line that
separates a tool from a plausible-sounding guess, and it is not negotiable.

## 2. Every output carries its lineage.

Each dataset MapSmith writes ships with a machine-readable manifest: input
files with checksums, the exact parameters used, the CRS decisions taken and
*why*, the engine and version that ran, timestamps. Everything needed to re-run the
analysis without a model in the loop is in there. And the chain of them is
recoverable from the last file alone, plan or no plan: one record does not point
at another, but each names the digests of its inputs, so hashing what you hold
finds what produced it and the walk continues until nothing claims the bytes. A
typed plan adds what the digests cannot say — what the analysis was for — and is
recorded with its own checksum. If you cannot reconstruct how a result was
produced, it is not a result. It is an anecdote.

## 3. Verify, then report. Not the other way around.

Every writer runs deterministic checks — CRS agreement, geometry validity,
count and extent invariants — and records them in the manifest **before**
raising anything. A failure that erases its own audit trail teaches you
nothing. The checks that failed are as much a part of the record as the ones
that passed.

## 4. Coordinate systems are stated, never assumed.

A silent CRS mismatch is the classic way a geospatial analysis comes out
confidently wrong: the arithmetic succeeds, the map looks plausible, and the
numbers mean nothing. MapSmith refuses inputs without a CRS, never runs metric
operations on degrees without a declared reprojection, and writes the reason
for every transformation into the manifest.

## 5. Model-agnostic by construction.

MapSmith is infrastructure, not a brain. It works with Claude, GPT, Qwen,
Kimi, GLM — anything that speaks MCP, cloud or local, today's models or next
year's. We will not ship a required model, because the moment a tool needs
its own weights it stops being infrastructure and becomes a stack you are
locked into.

The corollary matters more: **the leverage is better contracts, not better
weights.** Typed plans instead of prose. Static validation that names the
exact step and argument that is wrong. Error codes stable enough to act on.
A searchable catalog instead of a wall of hundreds of tools. Every one of
those improvements makes *any* model better at geoprocessing, and costs
nothing to maintain when the models change — which they will, faster than
any fine-tune can follow.

## 6. Few tools, deep capability.

Agent accuracy collapses when you hand it hundreds of near-identical tools.
MapSmith exposes a small set of goal-level operations and puts the breadth in
a searchable catalog the agent queries when it needs something — progressive
discovery instead of an overwhelming menu. Where several engines can do the
same job, the agent asks for the *operation* and MapSmith routes it; which
engine actually ran goes in the manifest.

## 7. Your data stays on your machine.

No telemetry, no phoning home, no dataset uploads: MapSmith runs beside your
data — on a laptop, in a container, on your own infrastructure. MapSmith itself
makes two outbound requests, and we would rather name them than have you find
them: the in-chat map panel fetches OpenStreetMap background tiles (which
reveals the map view you are looking at, and falls back to a plain background
when the host blocks it), and the SQL engine downloads its spatial extension
once per environment. Neither carries your datasets, and both are avoidable —
skip the panel, pre-install the extension. What an *agent* can reach through
the SQL engine is a separate question, answered precisely in `SECURITY.md`.
The provenance manifests MapSmith produces belong to you, and they happen to be exactly
the kind of record an audit asks for: what ran, on what inputs, with what
parameters, verified how. The EU AI Act's traceability obligations for
high-risk systems are not a burden if your tooling produces that trail as a
side effect of working correctly.

## 8. We publish the measurements, including the ones that disappoint us.

Claims about agent performance are cheap. MapSmith's benchmark work is public
— methodology, harness, raw approach, and results — including the experiment
where our own idea produced no measurable improvement and we said so. A
project that only reports its wins is asking for trust it has not earned.

---

MapSmith is AGPL-3.0 and always will be self-hostable. If it helps you sign
your name under an analysis with a straight face, it is doing its job.
